front: Which graph traversal guarantees the shortest path (by edge count) in an unweighted graph?
BFS uses which data structure to track what to visit next? DFS?
back: BFS uses a queue (FIFO). DFS uses a stack (LIFO), often implicit via recursion.

front: Time complexity of both BFS and DFS?
back: Θ(V + E) — every vertex visited once, every edge examined once (twice for undirected graphs).

front: Adjacency list vs. adjacency matrix: space complexity of each?
back: Adjacency list: Θ(V+E), good for sparse graphs. Adjacency matrix: Θ(V²), O(1) edge lookup but wasteful for sparse graphs.

front: What graph structure is topological sort only defined for?
back: A DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) — a cycle makes a consistent 'before/after' ordering impossible.

front: How does DFS-based topological sort build the ordering?
back: Each time a vertex finishes (all its descendants processed), insert it at the FRONT of a linked list. Θ(V+E) total.

front: Which edge types can appear in an UNDIRECTED graph's DFS? Which can't?
back: Only tree edges and back edges are possible — forward and cross edges can't occur, since every edge is encountered from both endpoints.

front: SCC algorithm: what are the three main steps?
back: 1) DFS(G) to get finish times. 2) Compute the transpose graph Gᵀ (reverse all edges). 3) DFS(Gᵀ) visiting vertices in descending finish-time order — each resulting DFS tree is one SCC.

front: Once every node has a (disc, finish) interval, how do you classify a non-tree edge (u,v) WITHOUT re-running DFS?
back: Compare intervals: v's interval nested inside u's (v a descendant) -> forward edge. u's interval nested inside v's -> back edge. Disjoint intervals -> cross edge. No other relationship is possible (parenthesis theorem).

front: Can adding a single edge to a directed graph ever SPLIT an SCC into more components? Can removing an edge ever MERGE two SCCs?
back: No to both. Adding an edge can only merge SCCs together (decrease or maintain the count); removing an edge can only split them apart (increase or maintain the count) -- never the reverse.

front: Eulerian circuit: what is the necessary condition on every vertex for one to exist?
back: In-degree must equal out-degree at every vertex (proof: if the circuit visits v exactly k times, it must use exactly k incoming and k outgoing edges there, and the circuit never reuses an edge).

front: The greedy 'always follow an unused outgoing edge' walk for finding an Eulerian circuit -- where does it always terminate?
back: Back at the start vertex -- never stuck elsewhere, because in-degree=out-degree guarantees an unused outgoing edge remains available at any non-start vertex the walk is currently at.

front: If the greedy Eulerian-circuit walk stops early (unused edges remain elsewhere), how do you extend it to a full Eulerian circuit?
back: Find a vertex on the current cycle with an unused outgoing edge, greedily walk a second cycle from there, then splice the two cycles together at their shared vertex. Repeat until no unused edges remain.
